title: Go SDK: streaming prefetch, cancellation tokens and deadline normalization
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Users of the Go SDK currently face awkward ergonomics when combining long-lived streaming RPCs with context cancellation and per-call deadlines. In practice we see two frequent pain points: (1) callers canceling contexts to stop reads while leaving goroutines blocked waiting for I/O or batching windows, and (2) mismatched timeout semantics between client-side deadlines and upstream server cancellation which leads to surprising retries or partial results.

Goal: Implement a client-side stream helper layer in the Go SDK that improves developer ergonomics by providing: a) optional prefetching/pipelining hooks that warm server-side KV cache and reduce first-response latency for next fragments, b) a cooperative cancellation token + backpressure token scheme that unblocks goroutines safely on cancel, and c) deadline normalization and propagation rules that avoid double-cancels and racey retries. Provide clear examples and tests demonstrating idiomatic usage patterns and migration guidance for existing users.
acceptance_criteria: Introduce a StreamHelper type in the Go SDK that wraps low-level stream connection and exposes Read/Recv with context-aware cancellation semantics.
Implement an optional prefetch mode that issues a low-priority prefetch request for the expected next range of tokens without violating rate limits.
Ensure cancellation via context cancels pending prefetches and unblocks pending Recv calls within 50ms on average in unit tests.

Normalize per-call deadlines: if client deadline is earlier than SDK-configured socket timeout, propagate the earlier deadline; avoid making the server see two independent cancels that trigger duplicate retries.

Provide 4 small example snippets in examples/ showing: graceful shutdown of a streaming consumer, cooperative backpressure, resumable stream reconnection with idempotent prepended tokens, and prefetch disabled for low-memory targets.
Add unit and integration tests covering deadline propagation, cancellation unblocks, and prefetch toggling, and show benchmarks comparing cold vs warmed prefix latency.
Documentation in the SDK changelog and Go examples updated with migration notes and recommended patterns.
Edge-case: when prefetch is enabled and connection fails, prefetch should not cause duplicated server-side state changes (prefetch must be read-only), verified by integration test harness.
tasks: Design API surface: StreamHelper struct, NewStreamHelper(opts...), WithPrefetch(bool), SetBackpressureWindow(int)
Implement cancellation coordination using a small in-process token (non-context) to allow explicit die/abort with fast wakeup of readers
Wire deadline normalization logic into the request layer and add telemetry for propagated vs default timeouts
Implement prefetcher that uses a low-priority async request path; ensure it respects global rate limiter
Add examples under examples/streaming/ demonstrating 4 patterns
Write unit tests for cancellation wakeups and deadline edge cases
Run integration tests against staging runtime to validate no duplicated side-effects from prefetches
Peer review and iterate with SDK maintainers and Runtime team
Add changelog entry and docs with migration guidance
notes_and_tradeoffs: Tradeoff: prefetch warms server-side caches and reduces tail latency for some workloads but increases network and server load; default off and opt-in per-stream.

We chose a cooperative in-process token rather than stuffing everything into context because context cancellation can be slow to surface across layered goroutines and may be used by callers for unrelated cancellation reasons.
Prefetch requests are strictly read-only and use a distinct trace/marker so the runtime can safely ignore them for billing/side-effect semantics; runtime changes required (see PR).
Backpressure window size default tuned to 3 next-fragment prefetches — empirically picked from benchmarks across text-completion and chat workloads.
We avoid automatic resumable stream heuristics that would mutate server state on reconnect; instead we provide an idempotent prepended token mechanism that calling code can opt into.
qa_and_testing: Unit tests: cancellation unblocks within expected time, prefetch toggles, deadline normalization logic
Integration: run against staging runtime to verify no duplicate side-effects and acceptable resource usage
Benchmarks: measure cold vs warmed prefix  p50/p95 latency on sample suite (news summarization, codegen prompts)
Fuzz: randomized cancel + reconnect sequences to validate no goroutine leaks
